questions.question: Using the scrap-metal smelter and the communal grazing field, explain the two market failures behind environmental deterioration and show why each produces overuse.
questions.expected_answer: Externalities: the smelter's ash imposes real costs — coughing children, ruined washing, spoiled gardens — on a township that never signed the transaction, so those costs reach no invoice; the steel rods are therefore priced too low, sell too fast, and the furnace runs longer than the full social cost would justify. The commons: the grazing field is owned by nobody, so each of the forty families captures the whole gain of one more cow while the thinner grass is a shared loss; every individually rational owner adds cattle and the field turns to dust — the tragedy of the commons. In both failures the market obeys prices that lie, and future generations, who buy nothing today, carry a price of exactly zero.

questions.question: Name the four families of environmental protection tools with a South African instrument for each, stating which failure each mends and one weakness of each.
questions.expected_answer: Command and control (emission ceilings, compulsory environmental impact assessments, fishing quotas and seasons) — imposes direct legal limits; certain, but only as strong as its inspectors. Market-based instruments (carbon tax, plastic bag and tyre levies, solar rebates, tradable permits) — replace the externality's zero price with a real cost so cutting pollution becomes cost-saving; efficient, but regressive on poor households unless revenue is recycled. Property rights and community management (community fishing rights, grazing committees, land-restitution parks earning tourism revenue) — give the commons an owner with a stake in its future; the initial allocation must be fair. International agreements (Paris Agreement) — stop free-riding because emissions cross borders; wide reach, weak enforcement. No family mends everything, so sound policy stacks them.

questions.question: Quote the Brundtland definition, apply the interest-versus-capital idea to one renewable and one non-renewable resource, and test the three pillars of sustainability against South Africa's just transition.
questions.expected_answer: Sustainable development 'meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. A fishery is renewable capital: harvested below its regeneration rate it pays interest forever; harvested above it the stock spirals down and behaves like a non-renewable. Platinum or coal is non-renewable: each ton is spent once, so sustainability means converting the once-off proceeds into durable assets — skills, infrastructure, diversified industry. Pillars applied to the just transition: environmental — decarbonise a coal-fired power system whose emissions also invite carbon border charges on exports; economic — build renewable capacity fast enough to keep production and jobs running; social — retrain coal workers and rebuild Mpumalanga's regional economy, part-financed by the roughly eight and a half billion dollars pledged under the Just Energy Transition Partnership. Drop any pillar — the climate, the power supply, or the coal towns — and the transition fails.
